summary: This proposed standard defines the Structure of Management Information for SNMPv2, which describes how managed objects and MIB modules are written, using a subset of ASN.1. It was replaced by RFC 1902.

plainLanguage.summary:
A network manager can ask a device for many things, and can tell it to change some of them. Every one of those values needs a written description so that both sides agree what it means.

This RFC defines that description language. It is a small, fixed subset of ASN.1, with three macros that cover a module of definitions, a single value the device exposes, and an unsolicited alert.

subtitle: The rules for writing down what a network device can report or be told, using a subset of ASN.1.

tldr.problem: Network management needs every managed object described in one precise, shared notation so that managers and devices agree on what each value means.
tldr.mechanism: The Structure of Management Information defines a subset of ASN.1 with three macros: MODULE-IDENTITY for modules, OBJECT-TYPE for managed objects and NOTIFICATION-TYPE for unsolicited notifications, plus rules for names, syntaxes, access levels and tables.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1442 was a Proposed Standard for SNMPv2 and was obsoleted by RFC 1902.

sections.title: What SNMP Management Information Is Made Of
sections.content:
A network management system contains several nodes, each with a processing entity called an agent that has access to management instrumentation, at least one management station, and a management protocol used to carry management information between the agents and the stations. The protocol's operations run under an administrative framework that defines authentication and authorization policies. Management stations run applications that monitor and control network elements, which are devices such as hosts, routers and terminal servers.

Management information is viewed as a collection of managed objects living in a virtual information store, the Management Information Base (MIB). Collections of related objects are defined in MIB modules, and those modules are written using a subset of OSI's Abstract Syntax Notation One (ASN.1). The purpose of this document, the Structure of Management Information (SMI), is to define that subset.

The SMI is divided into three parts. Module definitions use an ASN.1 macro, MODULE-IDENTITY, to convey the semantics of an information module. Object definitions use OBJECT-TYPE to convey the syntax and semantics of a managed object. Notification definitions use NOTIFICATION-TYPE to convey the syntax and semantics of an unsolicited transmission of management information.

The RFC also fixes the terminology: the original Internet-standard Network Management Framework, described in RFC 1155, RFC 1157 and RFC 1212, is called the SNMP version 1 framework, and the current framework is the SNMP version 2 framework.
sections.plainLanguage: SNMP has agents on the devices and stations that collect information from them. Every value a device exposes is a managed object, and the SMI is the notation used to write down what each managed object is.

sections.title: The Macros and the Information Module
sections.content:
An information module is an ASN.1 module defining information relating to network management. The SMI describes how to use a subset of ASN.1 to write one, and places further restrictions on standard modules, which enterprise-specific modules are strongly recommended to follow. There are typically three kinds: MIB modules, which define interrelated managed objects and use OBJECT-TYPE and NOTIFICATION-TYPE; compliance statements for MIB modules, which use the MODULE-COMPLIANCE and OBJECT-GROUP macros; and capability statements for agent implementations, which use the AGENT-CAPABILITIES macros. The classification is not a rigid taxonomy, and a standard module may not contain capability statements.

Every information module starts with exactly one invocation of the MODULE-IDENTITY macro, which must appear immediately after any IMPORTS or EXPORTs statements. That macro carries a LAST-UPDATED clause with the date and time of the last edit, an ORGANIZATION clause naming the organisation under whose auspices the module was developed, a CONTACT-INFO clause with the name, postal address, telephone number and electronic mail address of the person to take technical queries, a DESCRIPTION clause giving a high-level description of the contents, and optional REVISION clauses, each with its own date and description, listed in reverse chronological order. The value of the macro invocation is an OBJECT IDENTIFIER, which can then be used to refer to the module authoritatively.

Each macro invocation takes the form <descriptor> <macro> <clauses> ::= <value>. A descriptor must be unique and mnemonic, must not exceed 64 characters, must begin with a lower-case letter, must not end with a hyphen and must not contain two hyphens in a row. The set of descriptors in all standard modules must be unique. By convention, the descriptor for an object whose syntax is Counter32 or Counter64 should denote plurality.

To refer to an object defined elsewhere, the IMPORTS statement must name both the descriptor and the module that defines it. Where two enterprise modules define objects with the same descriptor, the ambiguity is resolved by prefixing the descriptor with the module name and a dot, as in module.descriptor. A module starts with one MODULE-IDENTITY invocation, and the OBJECT-TYPE macro defines a managed object with a SYNTAX clause, a MAX-ACCESS clause, a STATUS clause, a DESCRIPTION clause and optional UNITS, REFERENCE, INDEX or AUGMENTS and DEFVAL clauses.
sections.plainLanguage: A MIB module is a text file that describes a group of values a device exposes. It opens with a MODULE-IDENTITY macro that records who wrote it and when, and then lists each value with an OBJECT-TYPE macro that says what type it is, whether it can be read or written, and what it means.

sections.title: The Naming Hierarchy
sections.content:
Managed objects are named by OBJECT IDENTIFIER values arranged as a tree. The root of the subtree administered by the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) for the Internet is internet OBJECT IDENTIFIER ::= { iso 3 6 1 }, so the Internet subtree of object identifiers starts with the prefix 1.3.6.1.

Several branches under that subtree are used for network management. The mgmt branch, number 2, identifies standard objects. The experimental branch, number 3, identifies objects being designed by working groups of the IETF; when such a module becomes a standard information module, its objects move under the mgmt branch. The private branch, number 4, identifies objects defined unilaterally, and the enterprises branch beneath it, number 1, is used among other things to let providers of networking subsystems register models of their own products. The SMI does not prohibit objects being defined in other parts of the tree.

The SNMPv2 part of the tree, snmpV2 at number 6, carries the transport domains, the transport proxies and the module identities: snmpDomains, snmpProxys and snmpModules.
sections.plainLanguage: Every value the SMI describes has a numeric name, and the numbers form a tree. The Internet subtree starts at 1.3.6.1. Standard objects live under number 2, and objects a single company defines live under the enterprises branch at 1.3.6.1.4.1.

sections.title: Syntax, Access and Status
sections.content:
The SYNTAX clause of an OBJECT-TYPE macro defines the abstract data structure for the object, and it must be one of the alternatives of the ObjectSyntax CHOICE. The simple types are INTEGER, OCTET STRING, OBJECT IDENTIFIER and the enumerated form of BIT STRING. The application-wide types are IpAddress, Counter32, Gauge32, TimeTicks, Opaque, NsapAddress, Counter64 and UInteger32.

Integer32 covers integer-valued information between -2147483648 and 2147483647 and is indistinguishable from INTEGER. UInteger32 covers 0 to 4294967295. Counter32 is a non-negative integer that increases monotonically until it reaches 4294967295 and then wraps to zero; a Counter has no defined initial value, so a single value has no information content in general, and a Counter32 object is always read-only and may not have a DEFVAL clause. Counter64 is the same idea with a maximum of 18446744073709551615, and a standard module may use it only if the information would wrap in less than one hour with the 32-bit type. Gauge32 is a non-negative integer that may rise or fall but never exceeds its maximum, and TimeTicks is a non-negative integer counting hundredths of a second modulo 2^32 between two epochs. IpAddress is a 32-bit Internet address held as an OCTET STRING of length 4 in network byte order, and an OBJECT IDENTIFIER value may have at most 128 sub-identifiers, each no larger than 4294967295. Opaque exists only for backward compatibility and must not be used for newly defined object types.

The MAX-ACCESS clause says whether it makes protocol sense to read, write and/or create an instance. The values are ordered from least to greatest: not-accessible, read-only, read-write and read-create. This is the maximal level of access and is independent of any administrative authorization policy. If any columnar object in a conceptual row has read-create, no other columnar object in the same row may have read-write.

The STATUS clause says whether the definition is current or historic. A value of deprecated means the object is obsolete, but an implementor may still want to support it to interoperate with older implementations. The DESCRIPTION clause must give all the semantic definitions needed to implement the object.
sections.plainLanguage: Each value has a type and a size. Counter32 counts up and wraps at 4294967295, while Gauge32 goes up and down but never passes its ceiling. The access level says whether a manager may read, write or create the value.

sections.title: Tables, Rows and Indexes
sections.content:
Management operations apply only to scalar objects, but it is convenient to impose an imaginary tabular structure on the ordered collection of objects in a MIB. This conceptualization is formalised with the OBJECT-TYPE macro, used to define both an object corresponding to a table and an object corresponding to a row in it. A conceptual table has the syntax SEQUENCE OF <EntryType> and a conceptual row has the syntax <EntryType>, where the entry type is a SEQUENCE with one member for each subordinate object. The MAX-ACCESS of conceptual tables and rows is not-accessible.

The INDEX clause must be present when an object corresponds to a conceptual row, unless an AUGMENTS clause is present instead, and it must be absent otherwise. It defines the instance identification information for the columnar objects subordinate to the row. The index must name objects whose values will unambiguously distinguish one row from another, and the syntax of those objects says how to build the instance identifier. An integer-valued index becomes a single sub-identifier, which works only for non-negative integers; a fixed-length string becomes one sub-identifier per octet; a variable-length string becomes one sub-identifier for the length followed by one per octet; an object identifier becomes one sub-identifier for the count followed by the sub-identifiers themselves; an IpAddress becomes four sub-identifiers in the familiar a.b.c.d notation; and an NsapAddress becomes one sub-identifier per octet. The IMPLIED keyword may appear at most once in an INDEX clause, applies only to a variable-length syntax, and may not be used where the string could be empty. Instances identified by an integer should be numbered starting from one.

The AUGMENTS clause is the alternative to INDEX. A row with INDEX is a base conceptual row, and a row with AUGMENTS is an extension of the base row it names; the instances of its columnar objects are identified according to the INDEX clause of that base row. A base row may be augmented by several extensions, and creating a base row implies creating its extensions. The typical use is a vendor adding columns to a table defined in a standard MIB.

Objects named in the INDEX clause that are also columnar objects of the same row are called auxiliary objects, and newly defined auxiliary objects are not-accessible. A row must contain at least one columnar object that is not an auxiliary object. Where rows can be created and deleted, there should be one columnar object with the syntax RowStatus and a maximal access of read-create, by convention called the status column of the row.
sections.plainLanguage: A MIB describes tables. Each row is identified by an index, which says which values together name that row, and each row has columns holding the individual values. A vendor can add extra columns to a standard table by pointing at the standard row with an AUGMENTS clause.

sections.title: Revising an Information Module
sections.content:
As experience is gained with a published module it may be desirable to revise it. The MODULE-IDENTITY invocation is updated first, usually by changing LAST-UPDATED and adding a REVISION and DESCRIPTION pair; the module's label is not changed. If any non-editorial change is made to any clause of an object assignment, the OBJECT IDENTIFIER value associated with it must change too, along with its descriptor.

An object definition may then be revised in a limited set of ways. A SYNTAX clause containing an enumerated INTEGER may gain new enumerations or have existing labels changed. A STATUS of current may become deprecated or obsolete, and deprecated may become obsolete. A DEFVAL clause may be added or updated, a REFERENCE clause may be added or updated, a UNITS clause may be added, a conceptual row may be augmented by adding new columnar objects at the end of the row, and entirely new objects may be defined with previously unassigned OBJECT IDENTIFIER values. If the semantics of any previously defined object change in any other way, its OBJECT IDENTIFIER must change as well. Changing a descriptor counts as a semantic change, because descriptors may be used in an IMPORTS statement. When a STATUS changes, the DESCRIPTION should be updated to match. Notification definitions follow the same pattern, with a REFERENCE clause as the only permitted revision.

Refining a syntax is also restricted. The primitive or application type must not change, and the table in Section 9 allows a range to be narrowed, an enumeration to have named values removed, a size to be narrowed, and a repertoire to be reduced. Nothing else may be refined.

The Security Considerations section of the RFC says only that security issues are not discussed in this memo.
sections.plainLanguage: When a module is revised, most edits are allowed in place. But if the meaning of an existing object changes, the object must be given a new number, so that managers built for the old meaning are not misled.
